content: Specificity is a statistical measure that evaluates how effectively a binary classification test identifies negative cases. It represents the probability that a test correctly classifies individuals who do not have a preclinical disease as negative. Specificity is expressed as a proportional measurement, often in percentage terms. For instance, in the context of a medical test designed to determine whether a person has a specific disease, the specificity of the test refers to the probability that the test will yield a negative result for individuals who do not have the disease. In other words, specificity is the proportion of true negatives among all negative cases in the population. It is an inherent parameter of the test itself. High specificity is particularly important in scenarios where the treatment or diagnosis could have harmful mental or physical consequences for the patient. A specificity of 100% indicates that the test identifies all healthy individuals as healthy. However, this maximum specificity can be trivially achieved by a test that simply classifies everyone as healthy, regardless of their actual condition. Therefore, specificity alone does not provide information about how well the test identifies positive cases. To fully evaluate a test's performance, it is also necessary to consider its sensitivity or the specificities for other classes. A test with high specificity is associated with a low Type I error rate, meaning it minimizes the likelihood of false positives. Specificity is sometimes mistakenly equated with precision or positive predictive value, which instead refer to the proportion of returned positive results that are true positives. This distinction is particularly important when the sizes of the classes being tested are significantly different.
